fields.explain:
Often found in instructions, schedules and work requests.
“～までには” adds personal emphasis/determination compared with “～までに”.
Not used with nouns expressing a length of time (3時間までに×); use a specific point in time or an event.

• Expresses a deadline: something must be completed before or exactly at that point (the point in time itself included).
• Different from ～まで (until/up to): ～までに targets a “deadline point” and does not express duration.
• Vる＋までに: “before (the time when) … happens”, often used to set a condition for preparation.
• Often used with verbs that express completion: 終える, 提出する, 着く, 用意する,…
fields.notes:
• The point in time can be an “event”: 試験までに, 雨季までに…
• When the timeline is vague, use “～頃までに” for flexibility: 今月末までに／今月末頃までに.
• In work emails, combine it with “必ず／遅くとも／目安として” to make the deadline clear: 遅くとも金曜までに。
mistakes: Wrong use with a length of time: 3時間までに終わる× → 3時間以内に終わる✓ or 3時間で終わる✓
Confusing ～まで with ～までに: 5時まで来て× (ambiguous meaning) → 5時までに来て✓
Wrong clause with Vる＋までに (using the past): 会議が始まったまでに× → 始まるまでに✓
The JLPT often tests the “deadline” nuance: choose ～までに when there are keywords like “by/no later than/before”.

fields.explain:
An action with a clear purpose, usually with a person/role who carries it out:私がNをAにします.
The noun with を is the target being changed; Aな is the desired new state.
In reminders/signs: 〜にしてください/〜にしましょう are polite and carry a nuance of suggestion/request.
Different nuance: 「Aにします」 (choose) vs 「Aにします」 (make into A). Tell them apart by context and by whether there is a を-target or not.
Used with abstract adjectives (簡単,便利,安全,重大) to talk about optimizing/standardizing.

Expresses an intentional act: changing the state/property of something to some na-adjective.
- Pattern: Nを Aな に します = Make N become A (actively, by the speaker/agent).
Used to “simplify”, “clean up”, “make safe”, “make quiet” a target:簡単・きれい・安全・静か…
Implies a desired goal/standard: the speaker sets the target state and brings it about.
Different from ～になります (natural/unintentional): ～にします emphasizes human intervention, choice and decision.
Also used when choosing an option (with nouns): Aにします “I'll choose A”. With な形容詞, the nuance is “adjusting something so it becomes A”.
fields.notes:
Some words also have a dedicated adverb form (うまく/きちんと), but 上手に/きちんと have the same adverbial function. Choose according to habit/collocation.
“静かにして”: a fixed command meaning “be quiet”.
“きれい” is a な形容詞 but is also a noun in some structures; as an adverb, always use “きれいに”.
The -的（的） group, such as 積極的・具体的, is often used naturally in the form “～的に”.
mistakes: Wrongly using い形容詞+ にする (incorrect). Correct: い形容詞+ くする; な形容詞+ にする.
Confusing を and が: it must be NをAにする (not NがAにする).
Confusing it with ～になる:要 distinguish intention (にする) vs natural change (になる).
Machine-translating it as “decide to be A” in every case: with な形容詞 it usually means “make something become A”, while “decide/choose” applies when it is used with nouns.

fields.explain:
Neutral; used in both spoken language and written language. To be more formal, you can use AかBかにつきましては…
In direct questions, か appears once before the second choice: Aですか、Bですか。
With long clauses, it is better to repeat everything in full before and after か for clarity.
Often used with は to turn the phrase “AかBか” into a topic: AかBかは〜

Presents a contrasting choice/possibility: “A or B (or C)”.
Used like “whether A or B” together with verbs of perception/uncertainty:分かる、決める、迷う、知る、調べる、考える.
When the second possibility is “not A”, you can use “AかAないか” or shorten it to “Aかどうか”.
In direct questions, “それとも” can be used to connect them: Aですか、それともBですか。
With nouns/na-adjectives, use the plain form before か:静かか静かではないか.
fields.notes:
With な形容詞/名詞, the negative form in a contrasting pair usually uses ではない／じゃない:静かか静かではないか.
The second choice can be left out when the context is clear:行くか（どうか）まだ…
In titles/tables, A/B are often written briefly:可/不可,賛成/反対.
meaning_vi: Choice question: …N1 or N2? (～ですか、～ですか)
explain: This is a choice question: N1 or N2.
For this kind of question, we usually answer by choosing one of the options the asker gives.
examples: 1. A: これは　しんぶんですか、ざっしですか。
B: しんぶんです。
A: Is this a newspaper or a magazine?
B: It's a newspaper.
2. A: あなたは　じゅうはっさいですか、はたちですか。
B: わたしは　はたちです。
A: Are you 18 or 20?
B: I'm 20.
mistakes: Confusing AかBか with AやB: か is an exclusive choice; や is listing.
Dropping the second か in long sentences causes ambiguity. Keep the structure balanced: AかBか.
Use かどうか when option B is “not A”, to avoid unnecessary repetition.
In direct questions, do not put か right after A: say “Aですか、Bですか” (not “Aか、Bですか”).

Used to reduce directness/negation and create a soft feeling.

～けど means “but/although…”. Used to connect two contrasting clauses, to soften a sentence, or as an opener leading into a request/suggestion.
Core meaning: mild contrast, a change of direction.
Conversational, natural nuance, softer than が; ですけど is polite.
Can be placed at the end of a sentence to “trail off”, to hint at something/sound gentle:今日はちょっと…けど。
fields.notes:
The first clause (before けど) can be a full clause or a noun/adjective phrase:学生ですけど…。
“Trailing off” with けど helps with politeness/reduces pressure:今日は無理ですけど…。
In polite emails you can use けれども/しかしながら (above N5).
mistakes: Wrong position of です: × です高いけど → correct:高いですけど。
Using けど in overly formal writing → consider using が/しかし.
Forgetting to conjugate for tense in the first clause: ×行くたけど→ correct:行くけど／行ったけど。

fields.explain:
Y is usually the speaker's volition/intention:行く／頑張る／続ける／構わない…
When Y is an objective fact, it can still be used if it states a “no effect” relationship.
Combine it with emphatic words (たとえ／いくら／どんなに／もし) to strengthen the supposition/intensity.
Distinguish it from ～てもいい: adding いい changes the meaning to “it is allowed/it's fine”.

• Main meaning: concession/hypothetical concession, “even if X, Y still…”; Y is not affected by X.
• Scope: can be purely hypothetical (not yet real) or real; different from のに (already real, contrary to expectation).
• Common structures: たとえ～ても, いくら～ても, もし～ても; Y often expresses volition/judgment/habit.
• Variants for permission/no problem: ～てもいい (permission), ～てもかまわない (no problem).
fields.notes:
• Adversative pattern in argumentation: 「Aても、Bと言えない」 to negate an inference.
• In ads/slogans: 「どれだけ動いても、快適。」 carries a nuance of a quality guarantee.
• When connecting several concessive clauses: 「安くても、軽くても、丈夫でなければ意味がない。」
meaning_vi: Expresses that things ~ that seem obvious do not actually happen. The ~ part can be an affirmative event as in examples ①②; it can also be a real event as in the example. This sentence pattern is used with words like もし・どんなに・いくら or question words as in examples ②④⑤.
examples: 1. ①後輩「明日雪がふったら、練習は休みですか。」
先輩【いや、雪が降っても、休みじゃないよ。」
Junior: "If it snows tomorrow, will practice be canceled?"
Senior: "No, even if it snows, there's no day off."
2. ②もし暑くても、仕事にはスーツを着ていきます。
Even if it's hot, I wear a suit to work.
3. ③この料理はかんたんです。初めて作っる人でもできます。
This dish is simple. Even someone making it for the first time can do it.
4. ④説明が難しくて、何回読んでも、意味が分かりません。
The explanation is hard to understand; no matter how many times I read it, I don't get the meaning.
5. ⑤山田「ケーキが好きなんでしょう？これ、全部どうぞ。」
トム「え、いくら好きでも、こんなにたくさんは食べませんよ。」
Yamada: "You like cake, right? Please have all of this."

mistakes: Confusing it with のに: if the sentence has a nuance of regret/going against expectation → choose のに, not ても.
Wrong form with な-adj/N: it must be で＋も (きれいでも), not にも.
Mixing up なくても vs the different structure も…ない; “even if not” is ～なくても, not ～ないでも (except in limited colloquial use).
JLPT: the trap of てもいい (permission) vs ても (concession). Keywords asking for permission/OK → てもいい.
